items.item: The hook's two-hour delay isn't really about the lineage query being slow to run -- the real cost is that nobody had ever run it before, so the tooling and the habit of running it didn't exist yet. Lineage-derived blast radius only pays off if someone actually reaches for it under pressure, which this topic frames as a practice, not just a capability.

A reader might assume the five-stage loop is strictly sequential with no overlap, but in practice triage and contain often run concurrently -- the Ops lead starts containing the known-bad part while triage is still determining the full scope, which is exactly why the roles need to be distinct people rather than one person doing everything in order.

Lineage-derived blast radius is only as correct as the declared dependencies themselves -- an asset graph with an undeclared or stale dependency edge will silently under-compute the blast radius, which is a real failure mode distinct from (and arguably worse than) the guessing this topic replaces, because it looks authoritative while still being wrong.

Quarantining a partition rather than deleting it has a real storage and query cost while the incident is open -- readers who don't know to filter it out could still read the bad rows unless the quarantine is enforced at the query layer (a view, a row-level flag), not just a note in an incident document.

at.step: Reveal: quarantine, then a targeted repair

items.item: The three named roles (commander, Ops, Communication) aren't a complete org chart for every incident -- Google's own account also names a Planning role for longer-running logistics; this topic names the three most load-bearing roles for a data-specific incident rather than the full Incident Command System roster.

Blameless doesn't mean consequence-free for the system -- the Google SRE Book's own framing is that a blameless postmortem can and should still call out exactly where a service needs to improve; the blame is withheld from the person, not from the broken process or missing safeguard.

A reader coming from topic 3's backfill mechanics might assume 'targeted backfill' here is identical to a scheduled catchup backfill -- the mechanism is the same (resumable, interval-scoped), but the trigger is different: an incident's targeted backfill is manually scoped to exactly the quarantined partitions, not to a contiguous missed range.

at.step: Reveal: quarantine, then a targeted repair

items.item: OpenLineage's own value proposition in this topic is specifically cross-tool lineage (Airflow, Spark, dbt, Flink all emitting to one standard), which is a different scope than the single-orchestrator asset-graph lineage this topic's own lab demonstrates -- naming it in Frontier rather than claiming the lab itself used it avoids overstating what was actually run.

The real lab's forty-dashboard asset graph deliberately uses a simple modular pattern (every seventh dashboard genuinely depends on the affected table) rather than a organic-looking random graph, so the exact affected count is independently verifiable by a reader rather than only trusted from the code's own assertion.

Asset-level ownership (naming who owns each asset so an alert routes to them directly) is named in CHAPTER.md's own scope but has no independent primary source quoted here -- it's this topic's own synthesis of the incident-command roles applied at the level of a single table rather than a whole incident, consistent with the chapter's pattern of recapping and recombining rather than sourcing every operational idea externally.
